newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium extends rally, nickel, copper weaker.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium extends rally, nickel, copper weaker.

text.p: LME aluminium kept up its relentless rise on Monday afternoon, ratcheting up to a 22-month high, but some of the other metals eased on profit-taking and trade selling.
Three months aluminium touched $1,747 per tonne, the highest since early October 1995, as tightness bubbled under the market. It ended the afternoon kerb $5 firmer at $1,744.
The cash/three months spread ended the day at a $6/$10 backwardation, some $3/$4 wider than on Friday.
A squeeze centred on August coupled with a steady erosion in inventories and upside options plays were helping the market extend its bull run despite overbought signals, analysts said.
LME stocks fell by 450 tonnes on Monday and since the beginning of the year they have declined by about one third, said analyst Martin Squires of broker Rudolf Wolff.
The market has the potential for more gains, especially in the run up to Wednesday's options declaration, but profit-taking is expected to come in at some point, traders said.
Zinc also finished the day stronger, adding $31 to $1,494 as borrowing interest in spreads underpinned prices.
The premium of cash over three month metal straddled $100, with September the focus of the tightness.
The bulk of it was in the September/October spread, which held firm at a $73 backwardation.

A stocks rise of 1,700 tonnes was seen as a one-off increase that would not dent the consistent erosion of inventories. LME stocks have fallen a total of 21 percent by the end of last week, Squires said.
Three month prices still had scope to climb to $1,530, the highest price seen since the market plunged last week, he added.
Other markets, however, did not fare so well.
Copper continued its short-term downtrend, losing grip of the $2,300 mark as stocks kept rising.
July's jump in LME inventories of 106,625 tonnes was the biggest ever monthly increase, analysts said.
On Monday they rose by 2,800 tonnes.
Prices shed $27.50 to $2,282, with support pegged at $2,270 and $2,250.
Nickel fell back under profit-taking after a strike at Canada's Falconbridge failed to spark interest. Only an extended strike would impact on the fundamentals, analysts said.
Trade selling hit tin, which lost $55 to $5,585 after several days of speculative gains.
Lead moved sideways again in a narrow range, ending $2 easier at $637.
Alloy closed slightly weaker at $1,530/35, down from $1,540.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
